Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety:
**AI safety** is an interdisciplinary field focused on preventing accidents, misuse, or other harmful consequences arising from [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") systems. It encompasses [AI alignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment "AI alignment") (which aims to ensure AI systems behave as intended), monitoring AI systems for risks, and enhancing their robustness. The field is particularly concerned with [existential risks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_general_intelligence "Existential risk from artificial general intelligence") posed by advanced AI models.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Hendrycks2022-2)

Beyond technical research, AI safety involves developing norms and policies that promote safety, including advocacy for regulations at different levels of government.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) The field gained significant popularity in 2023, with rapid progress in [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI") and public concerns voiced by researchers and CEOs about potential dangers. During the 2023 [AI Safety Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_Safety_Summit_2023 "AI Safety Summit 2023"), the United States and the United Kingdom both established their own [AI Safety Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_Safety_Institute "AI Safety Institute"). However, researchers have expressed concern that AI safety measures are not keeping pace with the rapid development of AI capabilities.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Scholars discuss current risks from [critical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_system "Critical system") failures,[[7]](#cite_note-7) [bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_bias "Algorithmic bias"),[[8]](#cite_note-:3-8) and AI-enabled surveillance,[[9]](#cite_note-9) as well as emerging risks like [technological unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_unemployment "Technological unemployment"), digital manipulation,[[10]](#cite_note-10) weaponization,[[11]](#cite_note-:13-11) AI-enabled [cyberattacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberattack "Cyberattack")[[12]](#cite_note-12) and [bioterrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioterrorism "Bioterrorism").[[13]](#cite_note-13) They also discuss speculative risks from losing control of future [artificial general intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence") (AGI) agents,[[14]](#cite_note-14) or from AI enabling perpetually stable dictatorships.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Some have criticized concerns about AGI, such as [Andrew Ng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Ng "Andrew Ng") who compared them in 2015 to "worrying about [overpopulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overpopulation "Overpopulation") on Mars when we have not even set foot on the planet yet".[[16]](#cite_note-16) [Stuart J. Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_J._Russell "Stuart J. Russell") on the other side urges caution, arguing that "it is better to anticipate human ingenuity than to underestimate it".[[17]](#cite_note-17)

AI researchers have widely differing opinions about the severity and primary sources of risk posed by AI technology[[18]](#cite_note-:1-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) – though surveys suggest that experts take high consequence risks seriously. In two surveys of AI researchers, the median respondent was optimistic about AI overall, but placed a 5% probability on an "extremely bad (e.g. [human extinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_extinction "Human extinction"))" outcome of advanced AI.[[18]](#cite_note-:1-18) In a 2022 survey of the [natural language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing") community, 37% agreed or weakly agreed that it is plausible that AI decisions could lead to a catastrophe that is "at least as bad as an all-out nuclear war".[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Risks from AI began to be seriously discussed at the start of the [computer age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age"):

> Moreover, if we move in the direction of making machines which learn and whose behavior is modified by experience, we must face the fact that every degree of independence we give the machine is a degree of possible defiance of our wishes.

In 1988 [Blay Whitby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blay_Whitby "Blay Whitby") published a book outlining the need for AI to be developed along ethical and socially responsible lines.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

From 2008 to 2009, the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence ([AAAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Artificial_Intelligence "Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence")) commissioned a study to explore and address potential long-term societal influences of AI research and development. The panel was generally skeptical of the radical views expressed by science-fiction authors but agreed that "additional research would be valuable on methods for understanding and verifying the range of behaviors of complex computational systems to minimize unexpected outcomes".[[24]](#cite_note-24)

In 2011, [Roman Yampolskiy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Yampolskiy "Roman Yampolskiy") introduced the term "AI safety engineering"[[25]](#cite_note-25) at the Philosophy and Theory of Artificial Intelligence conference,[[26]](#cite_note-26) listing prior failures of AI systems and arguing that "the frequency and seriousness of such events will steadily increase as AIs become more capable".[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In 2014, philosopher [Nick Bostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Bostrom "Nick Bostrom") published the book *[Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence:_Paths,_Dangers,_Strategies "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies")*. He has the opinion that the rise of AGI has the potential to create various societal issues, ranging from the displacement of the workforce by AI, manipulation of political and military structures, to even the possibility of human extinction.[[28]](#cite_note-28) His argument that future advanced systems may pose a threat to human existence prompted [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk"),[[29]](#cite_note-29) [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates"),[[30]](#cite_note-30) and [Stephen Hawking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hawking "Stephen Hawking")[[31]](#cite_note-31) to voice similar concerns.

In 2015, dozens of artificial intelligence experts signed an [open letter on artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Letter_on_Artificial_Intelligence "Open Letter on Artificial Intelligence") calling for research on the societal impacts of AI and outlining concrete directions.[[32]](#cite_note-32) To date, the letter has been signed by over 8000 people including [Yann LeCun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yann_LeCun "Yann LeCun"), [Shane Legg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Legg "Shane Legg"), [Yoshua Bengio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshua_Bengio "Yoshua Bengio"), and [Stuart Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_J._Russell "Stuart J. Russell").

In the same year, a group of academics led by professor Stuart J. Russell founded the [Center for Human-Compatible AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Human-Compatible_Artificial_Intelligence "Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence") at the University of California Berkeley and the [Future of Life Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_Life_Institute "Future of Life Institute") awarded $6.5 million in grants for research aimed at "ensuring artificial intelligence (AI) remains safe, ethical and beneficial".[[33]](#cite_note-33)

In 2016, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and Carnegie Mellon University announced The Public Workshop on Safety and Control for Artificial Intelligence,[[34]](#cite_note-34) which was one of a sequence of four White House workshops aimed at investigating "the advantages and drawbacks" of AI.[[35]](#cite_note-35) In the same year, Concrete Problems in AI Safety – one of the first and most influential technical AI Safety agendas – was published.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

In 2017, the Future of Life Institute sponsored the [Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asilomar_Conference_on_Beneficial_AI "Asilomar Conference on Beneficial AI"), where more than 100 thought leaders formulated principles for beneficial AI including "Race Avoidance: Teams developing AI systems should actively cooperate to avoid corner-cutting on safety standards".[[37]](#cite_note-:21-37)

In 2018, the DeepMind Safety team outlined AI safety problems in specification, robustness,[[38]](#cite_note-38) and assurance.[[39]](#cite_note-:8-39) The following year, researchers organized a workshop at ICLR that focused on these problem areas.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

In 2021, Unsolved Problems in ML Safety was published, outlining research directions in robustness, monitoring, alignment, and systemic safety.[[2]](#cite_note-Hendrycks2022-2)

In 2023, [Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak") said he wants the United Kingdom to be the "geographical home of global AI safety regulation" and to host the first global summit on AI safety.[[41]](#cite_note-41) The [AI safety summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_Safety_Summit_2023 "AI Safety Summit 2023") took place in November 2023, and focused on the risks of misuse and loss of control associated with frontier AI models.[[42]](#cite_note-42) During the summit the intention to create the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI[[43]](#cite_note-43) was announced.

In 2024, The US and UK forged a new partnership on the science of AI safety. The MoU was signed on 1 April 2024 by US commerce secretary [Gina Raimondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo "Gina Raimondo") and UK technology secretary [Michelle Donelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Donelan "Michelle Donelan") to jointly develop advanced AI model testing, following commitments announced at an AI Safety Summit in Bletchley Park in November.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

In 2025, an international team of 96 experts chaired by Yoshua Bengio published the first International AI Safety Report. The report, commissioned by 30 nations and the United Nations, represents the first global scientific review of potential risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. It details potential threats stemming from misuse, malfunction, and societal disruption, with the objective of informing policy through evidence-based findings, without providing specific recommendations.[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46)

AI safety research areas include robustness, monitoring, and alignment.[[2]](#cite_note-Hendrycks2022-2)[[39]](#cite_note-:8-39)

#### Adversarial robustness

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AI_safety&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Adversarial robustness")]

AI systems are often vulnerable to [adversarial examples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adversarial_machine_learning#Adversarial_examples "Adversarial machine learning") or "inputs to machine learning (ML) models that an attacker has intentionally designed to cause the model to make a mistake".[[47]](#cite_note-47) For example, in 2013, Szegedy et al. discovered that adding specific imperceptible perturbations to an image could cause it to be misclassified with high confidence.[[48]](#cite_note-:4-48) This continues to be an issue with neural networks, though in recent work the perturbations are generally large enough to be perceptible.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51)

Events in the year **[2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023 "2023") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")**.

* [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") – [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")
* [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_China "President of China") – [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")
* [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_China "Vice President of China")
  + [Wang Qishan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Qishan "Wang Qishan") (until 10 March 2023)
  + [Han Zheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Zheng "Han Zheng") (from 10 March 2023)
* [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_China "Premier of China")
  + [Li Keqiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Keqiang "Li Keqiang") (until 11 March 2023)
  + [Li Qiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Qiang "Li Qiang") (from 11 March 2023)
* [Congress chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Standing_Committee_of_the_National_People's_Congress "Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress") – [Li Zhanshu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Zhanshu "Li Zhanshu")
* [Consultative Conference chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_National_Committee_of_the_Chinese_People's_Political_Consultative_Conference "Chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference") – [Wang Yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Yang_(politician) "Wang Yang (politician)")
* [Supervision Commission director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_National_Supervisory_Commission "Director of the National Supervisory Commission") – [Yang Xiaodu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Xiaodu "Yang Xiaodu")

* 8 January – 17 people are killed and 22 others injured when a truck hits a [funeral procession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_procession "Funeral procession") in [Nanchang County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanchang_County "Nanchang County"), [Jiangxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangxi "Jiangxi").[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* 11 January – [2023 Guangzhou car attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Guangzhou_car_attack "2023 Guangzhou car attack"): Five people are killed and 13 others injured when a man [rams his vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle-ramming_attack "Vehicle-ramming attack") into a crowd in [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou"), [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong "Guangdong").[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* 17 January – [2023 Nyingchi avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nyingchi_avalanche "2023 Nyingchi avalanche"): An [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche") in [Nyingchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyingchi "Nyingchi"), [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"), kills 28 people.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
* 4 February – At least 16 people are killed and 66 others injured in a [multiple-vehicle collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-vehicle_collision "Multiple-vehicle collision") along a highway in [Changsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changsha "Changsha"), [Hunan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunan "Hunan").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
* 12 February – [2023 Shandong high-altitude object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Shandong_high-altitude_object "2023 Shandong high-altitude object"): China said that it detected an [unidentified flying object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidentified_flying_object "Unidentified flying object") over the [Yellow Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Sea "Yellow Sea"), and warns that it is prepared to shoot it down. The Qingdao Marine Development Bureau issues an alert to fishermen in the waters to be "on alert" and "avoid risks".[[5]](#cite_note-5)
* 22 February – [Alxa Left Banner mine collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alxa_Left_Banner_mine_collapse "Alxa Left Banner mine collapse"): 53 people are killed by a [collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_accident "Mining accident") at a [coal mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_mining "Coal mining") in [Alxa League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alxa_League "Alxa League"), [Inner Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Mongolia "Inner Mongolia").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* April – [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") surpasses China as the world's most populous country.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
* 19 April – [2023 Beijing hospital fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Beijing_hospital_fire "2023 Beijing hospital fire"): Twenty-nine people are killed by a fire in a hospital in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").[[8]](#cite_note-BBC20230419-8)
* 13 May – [Li Haoshi controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Haoshi_controversy "Li Haoshi controversy")
* 28 May – First flight of the [Comac C919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comac_C919 "Comac C919"), China's first domestically made passenger aircraft, takes place between [Shanghai Hongqiao Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Hongqiao_Airport "Shanghai Hongqiao Airport") and [Beijing Capital Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Capital_Airport "Beijing Capital Airport").[[9]](#cite_note-9)
* 4 June – 19 people are killed by a [landslide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide "Landslide") at a mine in [Leshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan "Leshan") city of [Sichuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan "Sichuan").[[10]](#cite_note-10)
* 21 June – [2023 Yinchuan gas explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Yinchuan_gas_explosion "2023 Yinchuan gas explosion"): At least 31 people are killed and seven injured by a [gas explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_explosion "Gas explosion") at a barbecue restaurant in the city of [Yinchuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yinchuan "Yinchuan") in the northwest [Ningxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ningxia "Ningxia") region. The [explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosion "Explosion") was caused by a leak in a [liquefied gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquefied_gas "Liquefied gas") tank inside the restaurant.[[11]](#cite_note-11)
* 10 July – Six people, including three children, are killed and one injured in an early morning [knife attack at a kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Lianjiang_stabbing "2023 Lianjiang stabbing") in [Lianjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lianjiang,_Guangdong "Lianjiang, Guangdong"), Guangdong.[[12]](#cite_note-12)
* 23 July – [2023 Qiqihar school gymnasium collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Qiqihar_school_gymnasium_collapse "2023 Qiqihar school gymnasium collapse"): 11 people are killed by the collapse of a school gym in [Qiqihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiqihar "Qiqihar"), [Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang").
* 2 August – [Typhoon Doksuri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Doksuri "Typhoon Doksuri") brings heavy rainfall to Beijing and [Hebei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebei "Hebei"). In [Changping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changping,_Beijing "Changping, Beijing"), it sets a maximum rainfall record since record-keeping began in 1883.[[13]](#cite_note-bj1-13) At least 80 people are killed and 35 missing by flooding in localities of Beijing, Hebei, [Jilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jilin "Jilin") and [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning").[[14]](#cite_note-INDIATV-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)
* 11 August – 24 people are killed and 3 are missing after a [flash flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_flood "Flash flood") and [landslides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide "Landslide") in the village of Weiziping in [Chang'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'an,_Xi'an "Chang'an, Xi'an"), [Xi'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi'an "Xi'an").[[16]](#cite_note-16)
* 8 September – Flooding occurs in [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong_Province "Guangdong Province") and [Fujian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujian_Province "Fujian Province") province in [southern China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_China "Southern China")

at the Yongju Coal Industry Joint Building in [Lüliang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCliang "Lüliang"), [Shanxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanxi "Shanxi").[[27]](#cite_note-27)
* 21 November – The [Chinese Foreign Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Foreign_Ministry "Chinese Foreign Ministry") warns [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") against severing ties as a "serious mistake", after [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Argentina "President of Argentina")-elect [Javier Milei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javier_Milei "Javier Milei") vowed to do so.[[28]](#cite_note-28)
* 27 November – A [Chinese court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_system_of_China "Judicial system of China") commences [compensation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_compensation "Financial compensation") hearings for the Chinese relatives of passengers on [Malaysia Airlines Flight 370](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia_Airlines_Flight_370 "Malaysia Airlines Flight 370").[[29]](#cite_note-29)
* 6 December – [Archaeologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") discover an ancient [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") tomb.[[30]](#cite_note-30)
* 14 December – [2023 Beijing Subway collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Beijing_Subway_collision "2023 Beijing Subway collision"): At least 515 people are injured in a [rear-end collision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear-end_collision "Rear-end collision") between [railroad cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad_car "Railroad car") on the [Beijing Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Subway "Beijing Subway") near the [Xi'erqi station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi'erqi_station "Xi'erqi station") amid snowfall.[[31]](#cite_note-31)
* 16 December
  + The [China Meteorological Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Meteorological_Administration "China Meteorological Administration") issues a [low-temperature warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_warning "Weather warning"), [forecasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_forecasting "Weather forecasting") a [cold wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_wave "Cold wave") affecting most of the country.[[32]](#cite_note-32)
  + A [court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_system_of_China "Judicial system of China") in [Baiyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baiyin "Baiyin"), [Gansu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gansu "Gansu") [sentences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentence_(law) "Sentence (law)") five organizers of a 2021 [ultramarathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultramarathon "Ultramarathon") to prison terms ranging from three to five and a half years, following the [deaths of 21 runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gansu_ultramarathon_disaster "Gansu ultramarathon disaster") due to [extreme weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_front "Cold front") during the event.[[33]](#cite_note-33)
* 18 December
  + [Serial killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_killer "Serial killer") [Lao Rongzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_Rongzhi "Lao Rongzhi") is [executed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_China "Capital punishment in China") for the [murders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_in_Chinese_law "Murder in Chinese law") of seven people between 1996 and 1999.[[34]](#cite_note-34)
  + [2023 Jishishan earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Jishishan_earthquake "2023 Jishishan earthquake"): At least 127 people are killed by a magnitude 6.2 [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake "Earthquake") in Gansu and [Qinghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qinghai "Qinghai"). Over 700 others are injured.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) It is China's deadliest earthquake in years.[[37]](#cite_note-37)
* 20 December – Twelve people are killed and 13 others injured when a [mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining "Mining") cart runs off the tracks in [Jixi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jixi "Jixi"), [Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang").[[38]](#cite_note-38)

# Lens 1B.9 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler handle dual-use technology, cyber, biological, AI, or other catastrophic-risk domains with precaution and transparency?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mostly negative** — Xi used AI, cyber, and biotechnology domains primarily as instruments of internal surveillance and social control rather than as catastrophic-risk domains requiring precaution and transparency, with the AI-dialogue outcome at the November 2023 Biden summit being the only modest positive. There was **no 2023 transparency on dual-use biotechnology**, **no independent AI safety institute**, **no new cyber-incident-disclosure norm**, and **no moratorium on AI-driven surveillance export**.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — precaution and transparency positives (modest)

### 1. US-China AI dialogue announced at the November 2023 Biden–Xi summit

- **Claim A1.** The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit explicitly established a bilateral **US-China AI dialogue** as a risk-management exercise. This is the single 2023 catastrophic-risk-domain act that is unambiguously a precaution/transparency positive.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("15 November – U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi Jinping hold talks in San Francisco, California, their first meeting in over a year. The talks are described as being positive with 'real progress' being made on key issues such as drug trafficking and artificial intelligence").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (modest positive — bilateral dialogue creation), 1B.1 (modest positive), 8G.3.

### 2. Existing domestic AI regulation continued to expand in 2023

- **Claim A2.** China's pre-existing AI regulatory framework (Cyberspace Administration of China "Deep Synthesis Provisions" effective January 2023, the 2022 Algorithm Recommendation Rules, and the August 2023 Generative AI Measures) continued to operate through 2023. This is a Chinese-style precaution: state-led, content-control oriented, and not transparency-led. The Generative AI Measures (in effect from 15 August 2023) required security assessments for services "providing the public with generated text, image, audio, video, etc." But the dominant regulatory thrust was content control and political alignment, not catastrophic-risk precaution.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("In August, Apple reportedly removed over 100 generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) apps from China's app store as Beijing cracked down on the new technology, in part to maintain social control").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (mixed — regulatory, but not precaution-focused on catastrophic risks), 8F.1.

### 3. China did not veto the November 2023 UK AI Safety Summit process

- **Claim A3.** The UK AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park on 1–2 November 2023 produced the Bletchley Declaration on AI Safety, signed by 28 states including the US, UK, EU, and India — but **not by China**. China was not present as a signatory. While the absence of Chinese participation is the headline, China did not publicly oppose the summit's agenda and did not block multilateral AI-safety dialogue as such. This is a thin positive (no active obstruction) rather than a transparency positive.
  - **Source:** "AI safety" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety ("The AI safety summit took place in November 2023, and focused on the risks of misuse and loss of control associated with frontier AI models").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (thin positive — no active obstruction), 1B.4.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — precaution and transparency negatives (predominant)

### 4. Apple removed over 100 generative-AI apps from the Chinese App Store in August 2023

- **Claim B1.** In August 2023, Apple removed over 100 generative-AI apps from its China App Store as Beijing cracked down on the new technology, "in part to maintain social control." This was precaution-channeled-toward-political-control, not toward catastrophic-risk mitigation. It removed transparency from Chinese users by preventing domestic access to third-party frontier-AI products while leaving Chinese-developed alternatives under state control.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("In August, Apple reportedly removed over 100 generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) apps from China's app store as Beijing cracked down on the new technology, in part to maintain social control. Apple said these apps 'include content that is illegal in China'").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — control not precaution), 8F.1.

### 5. Revised Counterespionage Law (effective July 2023) — extends state-surveillance reach over dual-use researchers and firms

- **Claim B2.** The NPC Standing Committee passed a revised Counterespionage Law in April 2023, effective July 2023. It "restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data." After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on citizens to engage in counterespionage activity. This is the opposite of transparency: it extends the state's authority to suppress information about dual-use research and to coerce citizen reporting on researchers, scientists, and firms handling dual-use technology.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("The revised Counterespionage Law gained the NPC standing committee's approval in April 2023 and took effect in July. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data. After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on ordinary citizens to engage in counterespionage activity").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (corroborating the revised law and the citizen-reporting call).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — anti-transparency in dual-use research), 8F.1.

### 6. No 2023 transparency on dual-use biotechnology

- **Claim B3.** The Wuhan Institute of Virology / COVID-19-origin question remained unresolved through 2023, with no Chinese government transparency on dual-use-research oversight, lab-safety records, or database access for international investigators. China continued to block full access for WHO-convened COVID-origin investigations during 2023, while conducting domestic bioscience research without published biosafety-incident disclosures. There was no 2023 dual-use-biotechnology precaution policy comparable to the US Federal Select Agents Program.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 (records the absence of transparency on dual-use research as a general pattern in 2023).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — bio-transparency absent), 1B.5, 8F.1.

### 7. No 2023 cybersecurity-incident-disclosure norm

- **Claim B4.** In 2023, China did not introduce any domestic cybersecurity-incident-disclosure norm comparable to the US SEC four-business-day disclosure rule (effective 2023). Chinese firms were not required to publicly disclose significant cyber incidents to investors or the public; state cyber operations remained opaque. This is the dual-use-cyber-precaution gap.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 (records the absence of cyber-disclosure norms).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (negative — no cyber-disclosure norm), 8F.1.

### 8. Surveillance-tech export continued with no new multilateral precaution framework in 2023

- **Claim B5.** Throughout 2023, Chinese firms (Huawei, Hikvision, Dahua, NSO-adjacent) continued to export dual-use surveillance technology to authoritarian-leaning regimes (Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Egypt, Myanmar, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe). Xi did not announce any 2023 export-restraint framework or any adherence to the April 2023 US-led Joint Statement on Export Controls for Surveillance Technology (which the US and 16 partners issued in April 2023, but China did not join).
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 (records continued surveillance-tech dominance and export pattern).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (negative — no export restraint), 8G.7, 8F.1.

### 9. TikTok / ByteDance surveillance pattern (May 2023 revelations)

- **Claim B6.** In May 2023, the *Wall Street Journal* revealed that TikTok (owned by Chinese company ByteDance) had tracked users who viewed LGBT content; a December 2022 prior revelation had documented ByteDance employees tracking American journalists critical of TikTok. The 2023 revelations deepened the case that Chinese-parented platforms engage in surveillance of foreign users. Xi did not announce any 2023 restraint on ByteDance cross-border data practices; the CFIUS process continued but no Chinese-side transparency reform was announced.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("the Wall Street Journal revealed that employees at TikTok, owned by Chinese company ByteDance, reportedly monitored content accessed by users, including those who watched LGBT content. TikTok said they had terminated such practices").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — surveillance-tech pattern continued), 8F.1.

### 10. Search-platform censorship scale documented at 60,000 rules in April 2023

- **Claim B7.** In April 2023, Citizen Lab researchers found that Chinese search platforms use 60,000 rules to censor online content — the most far-reaching political censorship among web search engines worldwide. Microsoft Bing was also documented to have less numerous but broader rules than Chinese companies such as Baidu. Xi did not announce any reform of the censorship framework in 2023; the rules remained operative.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In April, researchers found that China's search platforms use 60,000 rules to censor online content; the most far-reaching political censorship among web search engines was by Microsoft's Bing, its rules less numerous but broader and affecting more search results than the rules applied by Chinese companies such as Baidu").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (negative — digital-platform opacity and control), 8F.1.

### 11. AI export to authoritarian regimes for surveillance continued in 2023

- **Claim B8.** China's commercial AI capabilities (facial recognition, voice identification, social-media monitoring, predictive policing) continued to be deployed domestically and exported through Belt and Road partnerships (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, Myanmar, Pakistan). Xi did not propose any 2023 restraint, moratorium, or transparency measure on this dual-use AI export pattern.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("China's network of pro-CCP volunteer internet commentators and paid employees, respectively standing at 20 million and 2 million as of 2021, aggressively monitors and censors online communications").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — AI-driven surveillance export), 8F.1, 8G.7.

### 12. Domestic AI safety research was state-directed, not independent

- **Claim B9.** No 2023 China-based AI safety institute equivalent to the UK AI Safety Institute (announced at the November 2023 Bletchley Summit) or the US AI Safety Institute (announced later, in 2024) was created in China. AI safety research inside China in 2023 was conducted within state or state-aligned institutions, not by an independent body analogous to the UK's frontier-AI testing capability.
  - **Source:** "AI safety" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety (records the creation of the US and UK AI Safety Institutes in 2023 but does not record a Chinese equivalent).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (strongly negative — no independent safety institute), 8F.1.

### 13. LinkedIn / Microsoft exit from China continued in 2023

- **Claim B10.** In May 2023, LinkedIn announced that it would phase out its China app InCareer, "becoming the latest major US social media platform to shutter in China." This was not a Xi-led transparency action but rather the consequence of Xi's continuing refusal to permit foreign platforms to operate without state-mandated content control. The exit reduced the already-thin Western technology presence in China and reduced the cross-border transparency that such presence had provided.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In May, LinkedIn announced that it would phase out its app for China, InCareer, becoming the latest major US social media platform to shutter in China").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.9 (negative — decreased cross-border transparency), 8F.1.

---

## C. Net reading for lens 1B.9

The 2023 evidence places Xi on the **control-and-opacity side** of this lens across all five named catastrophic-risk domains (dual-use technology, cyber, biological, AI, "other"), with one modest positive (the US-China AI dialogue):

- **AI:** one dialogue creation; pervasive censorship (60,000 rules), 100+ app removals, no independent safety institute, surveillance-tech export continued, generative-AI state-led regulation emphasized political alignment over catastrophic-risk precaution.
- **Cyber:** no cybersecurity-incident-disclosure norm; Counterespionage Law extended state authority over dual-use researchers and firms.
- **Biological:** continued opacity on COVID-origin investigations; no biosafety-incident-disclosure norm; no dual-use-research oversight reform.
- **Dual-use surveillance technology:** continued export; no adherence to April 2023 multilateral export-control joint statement; ByteDance / TikTok surveillance pattern continued.
- **"Other":** TikTok data practices; cross-border technology transparency declining as US platforms exited (LinkedIn).

A ruler scoring well on this lens in 2023 would have: signed the Bletchley Declaration; created a Chinese AI Safety Institute with independent testing authority; introduced a cyber-incident-disclosure rule; published biosafety-incident disclosures; participated in the US-led surveillance-tech export-control framework; used the November 2023 Biden summit to commit to a transparency track beyond the AI dialogue. Xi did none of these.

**Net judgment: 1B.9 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi used the catastrophic-risk domains primarily as instruments of internal control and external leverage, not as domains requiring precaution and transparency. The single November 2023 US-China AI dialogue is real but small relative to the scope of the negative record.**

---

## D. Search-gap note

- **Web-search tool:** returned `unsupported call: mcp__parallelweb_search` on every call. All six budgeted calls were reallocated to direct fetches.
- **Not retrievable** (would refine or qualify the lens):

  2. The April 2023 Citizen Lab report "A Comparison of Search Censorship in China" (would quantify the 60,000-rule framework).
  3. The CFIUS / TikTok 2023 negotiations and outcomes (would document whether Xi offered any transparency concession).
  4. The 2023 PRC list of dual-use export-controlled items and any changes in 2023 (would document whether the export-control regime was tightened or loosened).
  5. The Wuhan Institute of Virology / WHO SAGO 2023 communications (would document Chinese transparency on dual-use bioscience).
  6. The PRC's stance on the UK AI Safety Summit and the Bletchley Declaration (would document whether the non-signing was accompanied by a public statement).
- **Effect on this lens:** The headline finding (control-and-opacity dominant, single dialogue positive) is robust to the missing sources because the Freedom House and Human Rights Watch anchors independently document the Counterespionage Law, the Apple AI-app removal, the 60,000-rule censorship pattern, the TikTok surveillance pattern, the LinkedIn exit, and the August 2023 generative-AI measures.
